summary:
Two separate criminal-law regimes apply across the Palestinian Territories, and the difference between them determines what a trans visitor faces. In the West Bank, criminal law derives from the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960. Jordan's 1951 revision of its own code dropped offences covering consensual private sexual conduct, and the 1960 code carried that position forward, so no provision there criminalises consensual same-sex acts. In Gaza, Criminal Code Ordinance No. 74 of 1936 remains the governing text. Section 152(2) punishes consensual same-sex "carnal knowledge" by up to ten years' imprisonment, and section 152(1)(c) sets up to fourteen years for sodomy with a child under sixteen. Neither code names trans identity. Gaza's public-morality provisions are the route by which trans people are brought within the criminal law, and the source material describes the resulting position as de facto oppression rather than formal prohibition.

The applicability of the 1936 ordinance is contested. Human Dignity Trust and Human Rights Watch hold it in force in Gaza; Amnesty International does not report same-sex acts as illegal there; the editor-in-chief Anis F. Kassim has argued the text could be read as permitting homosexuality. Palestinian law overall is a patchwork of Ottoman, British, Jordanian, Egyptian and Israeli legacies, and the Palestinian Authority has legislated neither for nor against homosexuality. Israel stopped applying the Mandate criminal code in 1977.

Enforcement against LGBT Palestinians is documented. Gay Palestinians are often arrested and tortured, and the Palestinian Authority's usual stated justification for persecution is to label the person a collaborator. Shaul Ganon of the Israeli rights group Aguda reported knowledge of two cases within a three-year window in which people were tried explicitly for being homosexual, and said that since the intifada, as police increasingly enforced Islamic law, being openly gay under the Palestinian Authority was not possible. Palestinian police banned LGBTQ activity, and after action against the organisation al-Qaws the group received a wave of hate messages that activists described as a serious threat.

No legal gender recognition provisions are set out for the Palestinian Territories, and no broad legal protections from discrimination exist for LGBTIQ+ people. The Palestinian Authority is not a signatory to key human rights treaties.

Social conditions are hostile. Palestine ranks 130 on the Global Acceptance Index with very little movement between 2010 and 2020. Interviews by Human Rights Watch and the Women's Centre for Legal Aid with twelve Palestinian women identifying as lesbian, bisexual or queer recorded widespread discrimination and abuse in public and in family settings. Social and family persecution makes the practical position harsher than the formal law in the West Bank.

Health care for trans and queer people is inadequate. HIV-positive people often do not receive continuous antiretroviral therapy because medication is limited and stigma is high, and comprehensive epidemiological surveillance is lacking. Ninety-eight HIV/AIDS cases were officially registered in Palestine between 1988 and 2017, seventy-nine of them AIDS and nineteen HIV-positive, with the true figure likely far higher because taboos obstruct data collection. In Gaza, the collapse of the health system and blockades since October 2023 have made access to life-saving HIV medication especially difficult.

Civil society groups that protect women and children in Gaza are described as vulnerable to attack.
tangentialFactors: Israel is the adjacent jurisdiction through which LGBT Palestinians most often seek protection, and the terms are restrictive. LGBT Palestinian asylum seekers in Israel are routinely excluded from basic healthcare programmes and shelter access available to other asylum seekers, and some have faced house arrest or deportation. Only in June 2022 did Israel begin issuing work permits to gay Palestinian refugees granted asylum and to those fleeing domestic violence. Around ninety LGBT Palestinians have received temporary permits to seek refuge in Israel after fleeing violence in the territories.
localsOnly:
Statelessness is cited as a structural condition of LGBTQ Palestinians.

Palestinian queer organisations operate from within Israel rather than from the territories, so residents have limited locally based advocacy or support structures.

Gay Palestinians are blackmailed into working as informants by Israeli security services, a pressure that operates alongside the Palestinian Authority's use of the collaborator label.
outOfScopeNotes:
A 2003 draft Palestinian penal code criminalised adult consensual same-sex conduct, with up to five years for male-male sodomy. Whether it was ever implemented is not established.

The account of arrests, torture and prosecutions attributed to Shaul Ganon rests on a single activist's knowledge of two cases and is not dated beyond a three-year window relative to its publication.

No legal gender recognition provisions are set out in the sources; this records the absence of published provisions rather than a documented prohibition.

Registered HIV figures for Palestine are a floor. The sources state that taboos obstruct data collection and that comprehensive surveillance is lacking, so the official total understates the true number.
